summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors and remains the most conservative country in its region. There is no legal gender recognition procedure in force: the judiciary has yet to issue final rulings on ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents.

The protection framework is empty. No anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and there is no hate-crime statute. Amnesty documents persistent structural discrimination, and AP reported in September 2025 that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work. The same reporting period records 37 registered feminicides in 2025.

Hostility reaches official institutions. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, and an April bill would merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family. Elite-level rhetoric is on record: ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes made a violent remark in 2017 about his son marrying a man, later apologising to those offended, within a political climate that included calls to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and there is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people. Asunción has a small organised community. Tourist traffic is low and the inventory contains no documented incidents involving trans visitors, so the operative risk is social hostility and the absence of any protection machinery rather than state persecution.

Partner recognition is also absent. Paraguay recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must permit same-sex marriage binds Paraguay as a party, but domestic law has not been adapted, and commentators inside the country describe the legislative work still required to extend marriage to everyone.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between the inter-American framework and Paraguayan statute is the clearest structural tension in the record: the advisory opinion is binding on the state, while local law continues to recognise only opposite-sex marriage, and domestic experts say the country must overcome political difficulty to close that gap.

Political rhetoric at the highest level sets the tone for street-level hostility. The 2017 statements attributed to Horacio Cartes and the reported campaign against books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology' indicate an elite climate in which anti-LGBT positions carry little political cost.

Feminicide figures and the proposed merger of the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family point to a broader weakening of gender-based violence machinery, which affects trans women disproportionately even where the statistics are not disaggregated by gender identity.
localsOnly:
Adoption law does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or single men and women: Law 1136/97 restricts adopters only on grounds of infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records, a statutory gap that permits same-sex adoption in practice while social barriers remain.

Residents seeking legal name recognition must proceed through the courts on a case-by-case basis, with the ten pending lawsuits showing that the process runs for years without final judgment.

Trans Paraguayans who leave their hometowns commonly relocate to the capital or abroad, and AP reporting links that internal displacement directly to discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence, with sex work a frequent survival strategy after migration.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcomes of the ten name-recognition lawsuits and of the UN Human Rights Committee communications are unresolved in the inventory; no source records a final ruling or Committee decision, so the current status of those cases is not sourced.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, passport or ID gender-marker rules for foreign travellers, or access to healthcare for visitors. Whether a trans visitor's documents are examined at the border, and on what basis, is not sourced here.

The claim that there is no documented pattern of police targeting rests on the absence of such reports in the available sources rather than on an affirmative official finding; the inventory contains no dedicated study of police conduct toward trans people.

Whether the April bill merging the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family has been enacted is unresolved in the inventory, which records the bill but not its passage.

Adoption practice is described from a 2017 legal analysis; whether courts or child-welfare agencies apply the statutory gap in current cases is not sourced.
